passage:
Subject: Could your clinic prepay for a year?

Dear Sachin,

Investor talks have dragged on for five months, and every meeting ends with "we'll get back to you". I realised I was waiting on other people for something my first customers might be able to help with.

Here is my idea. If ten clinics like yours paid for a year up front, at a lower rate than usual, that would cover one developer and the servers without any investor. Growth would be slower, but we would decide what to build. If we ever failed to deliver, the unused part would be refunded.

I feel a bit nervous asking, but I would rather ask than assume. Could we talk this week?

Jahnavi

qa.q: How long have the investor talks dragged on?
qa.a: They have dragged on for five months.

qa.q: How does Jahnavi feel about asking Sachin?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels nervous but hopeful, saying so directly and choosing to ask rather than assume.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi do if only a few clinics agree to prepay?
qa.a: Jahnavi could start with a smaller plan that those clinics cover, and use the results to ask more clinics later.

qa.q: What might Sachin weigh before agreeing to prepay?
qa.a: Sachin might weigh whether the tool is worth paying for a year ahead and whether the refund promise is enough if delivery slips.

grounding: The email shows a founder, with investor talks dragging, asking early customers about prepaid contracts and a slower path that keeps more control.

passage:
Sonali, everyone expects me to say we raised a big round. We didn't. I'm Zainab, and after eight months of investor talks that ended in "let's catch up next quarter", I got tired of waiting in lobbies. One night I asked a different question: what if our customers could fund us instead?
Our clients are schools. They buy for the whole year anyway. So I went to our twelve happiest schools and offered a discount if they paid for the year upfront. Seven said yes. That money paid for two developers and a year of servers.
Is it slower than a big round? Yes. We grow maybe a third as fast. But nobody sits on my board, nobody pushes me toward a market I don't believe in, and every rupee came from someone who actually uses what we make. I'll take that, Sonali.

qa.q: How many schools agreed to pay upfront?
How does Zainab feel about the slower path?
qa.a: Zainab feels content and in control, even proud, preferring steady customer money to waiting on investors.

qa.q: What else could Zainab do to keep this path working?
qa.a: Look after the prepaid schools closely so they renew, and offer the same deal to a few more happy schools.

qa.q: How might the seven schools see the upfront deal?
qa.a: They get a discount on something they buy yearly anyway, and a supplier who depends on keeping them happy.

grounding: It shows a founder, tired of slow investor talks, getting early customers to prepay yearly contracts and choosing a smaller, steadier path that keeps control.

passage:
I've worked with Zubin since his catering-software company had three people, so I watched the fundraising drag on through the whole monsoon. Meeting after meeting, investors said, "Promising, come back in a quarter." Zubin looked more tired every week.
Then in September he tried something different. He called our biggest restaurant-chain clients and asked whether they would pay a year in advance if we built the two features they kept asking for. I sat in on one call. He was nervous; I could see his knee bouncing. Three of five chains said yes.
With that money we hired one developer and built the features. We're growing more slowly than the funded startups I read about. But Zubin stopped living in investor lobbies, and last week he told me, "At least now the company is ours." I'm not sure he is completely at peace with slower. But he looks calmer.
— Pallavi

qa.q: How many chains agreed to pay in advance?
What does Zubin's bouncing knee suggest?
qa.a: He was nervous during the call, unsure whether the clients would agree.

qa.q: What could Zubin do to make the prepaid path last?
qa.a: Deliver the two features on time and ask the chains for feedback, so they renew next year.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see the change in Zubin?
qa.a: Pallavi sees him calmer and more in control, though not sure he is fully at peace with slower growth.

grounding: It shows a founder turning from dragging investor talks to prepaid contracts from existing clients, accepting slower growth that keeps control of the company.
